metadata.title: Job satisfaction predicts teacher self-efficacy and the association is invariant: Examinations using TALIS 2018 data and longitudinal Croatian data

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: Study 1 uses OECD TALIS 2018 teacher survey data from 46 OECD countries/economies with a hierarchical structure (teachers nested in schools nested in countries). The paper does not report the use of TALIS sampling weights or any specific weight variable (e.g., TOTWGT or W_FSTUWT), and the analyses are conducted in Mplus using TYPE=COMPLEX to adjust standard errors for clustering complexity rather than applying explicit survey weights. Study 2 uses a convenience sample of 3002 Croatian teachers from 135 state schools; the paper does not describe any probability-sampling weights for this national longitudinal dataset. Missingness is handled via FIML in Mplus, which is a model-based approach for incomplete data rather than a weight-based correction.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values are not applicable because the dependent variables are teacher self-efficacy and job satisfaction latent constructs measured via questionnaire Likert items, not cognitive achievement scores with PVs. Missing data handling is implemented using full information maximum likelihood (FIML) in Mplus, which is treated here as a model-based multiple-imputation-like approach for incomplete data under the authors’ specified likelihood framework.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Study 1 (TALIS 2018): the authors used TALIS country cases adjudicated as valid by OECD and retained only countries/economies that contained data on both teacher self-efficacy (TSE) and job satisfaction (JS), resulting in 46 countries/economies and 252,881 unique teacher responses. Teachers were further categorized by gender, career stage (early/mid/late based on years of teaching experience), and ISCED educational level taught; TALIS PISA link cases were excluded when analyzing educational level because ISCED levels for those link cases were not available. Study 2 (Croatia longitudinal): a convenience sample of 3002 teachers from 135 Croatian state schools participated in a three-wave full-panel design with six-month lags (Autumn 2015, Spring 2016, Autumn 2016). Attrition occurred across waves (only 1525 at Time 2 and 1081 at Time 3), and the authors conducted an attrition analysis and then used FIML to handle missingness rather than restricting to complete cases.

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS 2018 data and longitudinal Croatian data
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 data and longitudinal Croatian the study leveraged Gender, Teaching experience (years), Career stage to predict predicted TSE at subsequent waves (b=0, finding that This paper is not an ML prediction study; it uses TALIS 2018 teacher questionnaire data (Study 1) and a three-wave longitudinal convenience sample of Croatian teachers (Study 2) to test cross-sectional associations and longitudinal cross-lagged relations between teacher self-efficacy (TSE) and job satisfaction (JS). In Study 1, the authors used confirmatory factor analysis and multi-group CFA to establish measurement and covariance invariance across gender, career stage, and educational level, reporting that the TSE–JS association is invariant across these moderators (fit indices such as CFI/TLI > .90 and RMSEA around .056–.059 in the reported models). In Study 2, they estimated autoregressive cross-lagged panel models (CLPM) with robust maximum likelihood (MLR) and found that JS at Time 1 and Time 2 significantly predicted TSE at subsequent waves (b=0.088 and b=0.142, p<.01), while TSE did not significantly predict future JS (b=-0.063 and b=0.029, p>.05). The study relies on self-report measures and uses FIML for missingness, but it does not report explicit survey-weight application for TALIS. This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.

data.null_fields_interpretation: The extraction is sparse for main_findings and ml_techniques because the article does not train or evaluate machine learning models; instead, it applies CFA/MG-CFA and cross-lagged panel modeling to test invariance and temporal ordering. Consequently, there are no ML target variables, predictive performance metrics, or algorithm comparisons to populate into the StructuredFinding schema.
